lesson.title: IPv4: The 32 Bit Addressing Scheme That Still Runs the Internet
lesson.summary: IPv4 is the connectionless, best effort network layer protocol from RFC 791 that identifies every internet endpoint with a 32 bit address, a design choice whose limited address space still shapes networking decades later.
lesson.body:
IPv4, or Internet Protocol version 4, is the network layer protocol defined in RFC 791 in 1981 that gives every packet crossing the internet a source and destination address and a best effort promise to deliver it, without any guarantee of delivery, ordering, or timing. It sits squarely at the network layer of the internet's layered design: below it sits the link layer, technologies like Ethernet cabling or a wireless medium that move raw bits across one physical hop, and above it sits the transport layer, where protocols like TCP and UDP add the port numbers, reliability, and flow control that IPv4 itself does not provide. IPv4 does not care what is inside a packet's payload, whether that is a TCP segment carrying a web page or a UDP datagram carrying a video stream, and it does not guarantee anything beyond attempting to route that packet toward its destination one hop at a time.

The defining and most consequential design choice in IPv4 is a 32 bit address field, which yields a theoretical maximum of 2 to the 32nd power addresses, a little over 4.29 billion. In 1981 that number felt effectively unlimited. It was not: decades of exponential growth in connected devices exhausted the pool of globally assignable IPv4 addresses, a shortage severe enough that IANA handed out the last unallocated top level blocks to the regional internet registries in 2011, which is precisely why technologies like NAT (network address translation) and the private IPv4 ranges defined in RFC 1918 exist, and why IPv6, with a 128 bit address space, was standardized as a long term replacement that has still not fully displaced IPv4 today.

IPv4 is connectionless, meaning it does not set up a dedicated path before sending data and treats every packet independently; a router examines each packet's destination address and forwards it based on its own routing table, with no memory of packets that came before it. This is what lets IPv4 scale to a global network with no central coordinator, since no router anywhere needs to track the state of an individual conversation, but it also means IPv4 by itself offers no reliability, no flow control, and no security, all of which are left to protocols layered on top of it, most commonly TCP for reliability and IPsec or TLS for security.

Every IPv4 packet carries its addressing and control information in a structured IPv4 header that precedes the payload, and understanding that header, how an IPv4 address is formatted as four octets, how those addresses were originally grouped into classes, which ranges are reserved for private and loopback use, and how a single address block can be subdivided into subnets, are all details that build directly on top of the basic IPv4 protocol described here. None of that machinery exists in isolation; it all exists to make the same 32 bit addressing idea usable at internet scale.
